name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,797

entries.clue: Johnny and Mark could be officially OK (6-5)

blocks.note: a johnny is British slang for a condom, also called a rubber
a stamp is a mark

annotation.surface: Someone mulls over whether a man called Johnny and his friend Mark would pass muster.
annotation.walkthrough: Johnny and Mark read as two men's names; both are ordinary nouns here, with johnny the British slang for a condom.
annotation.definitionFit: To rubber-stamp something is to approve it officially, often without scrutiny.

entries.clue: Possibly put a cap on shivering critters? (8)

indicatorNotes.shivering: shivering creatures tremble, so their letters are shaken up

blocks.note: the letters of CRITTERS rearranged

annotation.surface: Someone wonders whether cold little animals might want woolly hats.
annotation.walkthrough: The cap looks like headgear for cold animals, but to put a cap on is to limit.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a cap is an upper limit, so putting one on a budget or a price is limiting it.

entries.clue: Totally support everyone in live format getting half cut (2,3,3)

indicatorNotes.in: ALL goes inside the other letters
indicatorNotes.half cut: FORMAT loses half its letters, leaving FOR

blocks.note: to live is to be
everyone is all
the first half of FORMAT

annotation.surface: A plea for everyone to back a live show format that is being trimmed, with a hint of drunkenness in 'half cut'.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Half cut' is British slang for tipsy, but here it just chops a word in two; 'live format' reads as a TV term but splits across the pieces.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: being 'all for' a plan means backing it without reservation, which is what 'totally' adds.

entries.clue: Listen with zeal to each plonk being brought over (3,2)

indicatorNotes.being brought over: brought over means turned round, so PUT becomes TUP

blocks.note: EA is the standard abbreviation for each
to plonk is to put down; PUT turned round

annotation.surface: Someone eagerly hears out each of their guests as the cheap wine is handed round.
annotation.walkthrough: Plonk is British slang for cheap wine, but here it is the verb meaning to set down heavily. To eat up someone's words is to listen avidly.
annotation.definitionFit: An audience that eats up a speech listens to it with relish.

entries.clue: More sentimental wimp must get support (7)

blocks.note: a sop is a weak, spineless person
a pier is a supporting pillar

annotation.surface: A wimp is told they need someone to lean on.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition hides at the front, where 'more sentimental wimp' reads as one phrase.
annotation.definitionFit: Soppy means mawkishly sentimental; soppier is its comparative.

entries.clue: A crew injecting heroin on a mountain top? (7)

indicatorNotes.injecting: the crew injects H, putting it inside

blocks.note: as printed
H is slang for heroin
a rowing eight is a crew

annotation.surface: A gang of addicts shooting up high on a peak.
annotation.walkthrough: H goes between A and EIGHT. AHEIGHT is an old adverb meaning on high, and the question mark flags a mountain top as just one example.
annotation.definitionFit: Aheight is an archaic word for aloft, so on a mountain top you are aheight.

entries.clue: A bloated criminal beneath bow of police vessel (5,4)

indicatorNotes.criminal: criminal suggests something bent out of shape
indicatorNotes.beneath: in a down entry, the anagram sits beneath P
indicatorNotes.bow of: the bow is the front of a ship, so its first letter

blocks.note: the first letter of police
the letters of A BLOATED rearranged

annotation.surface: A fat crook is found lurking under the front of a police launch.
annotation.walkthrough: Bow and vessel both fit the nautical picture, but bow only means the front letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A pedal boat is a small craft driven by pedals, and any boat is a vessel.

entries.clue: Welsh earl heading to major Shropshire town (3)

indicatorNotes.heading to: the heading of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: W is the standard abbreviation for Welsh
E is the standard abbreviation for earl
the first letter of major

annotation.surface: A Welsh nobleman sets off for the county's big town.
annotation.walkthrough: Shropshire is an English county on the Welsh border; Wem is a small market town there, so 'major' is a joke.
annotation.definitionFit: A proper name: the answer is a small market town north of Shrewsbury, in the English county on the Welsh border.

entries.clue: Piece of seafood sparkles after being shelled (6)

indicatorNotes.after being shelled: shelling strips the outside, so the outer letters go

blocks.note: TWINKLES without its first and last letters

annotation.surface: A bit of seafood glistens once it has been taken out of its shell.
annotation.walkthrough: Shelling suits seafood perfectly, which hides that it is stripping TWINKLES of its outer letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A winkle is a small edible sea snail.

entries.clue: After dumping soldiers, recollect one of many here? (6)

indicatorNotes.After dumping: dumping means throwing out, so RE is dropped

blocks.note: RE is the Royal Engineers
to recollect is to remember

annotation.surface: Someone who has dumped their army mates tries to recall whether they were one of the crowd.
annotation.walkthrough: REMEMBER minus RE leaves MEMBER. 'Here' points at the word itself: a member of 'many' is one of them.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: any single person belonging to a large body, such as Parliament, is one of its many.

entries.clue: A vertical passageway? Quiet at the back! (5)

blocks.note: sh is a call for quiet
aft means at the back of a ship

annotation.surface: A teacher asks what a vertical passageway is, then snaps at the chatterers in the back row.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Quiet at the back!' reads as a teacher's command; aft is the nautical word for the rear of a ship.
annotation.definitionFit: A mine or lift shaft is a vertical passage.

entries.clue: My nude pose mostly excited Hoskins, for example (9)

indicatorNotes.mostly: mostly means all but the last letter

blocks.note: as printed
POSE without its last letter

annotation.surface: The setter owns up to being aroused by their own naked photo shoot.
annotation.walkthrough: Hoskins is the setter's own name, so this refers to itself: a crossword alias is a pseudonym.
annotation.definitionFit: Hoskins is the pen name this setter uses.

entries.clue: A pilsner drunk by German back on the sauce? (9)

indicatorNotes.drunk: drunk letters stagger out of order

blocks.note: the letters of A PILSNER rearranged
G is the standard abbreviation for German

annotation.surface: A German who had quit drinking is spotted downing a lager.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Back' belongs to the definition, not to G; 'on the sauce' is slang for drinking alcohol.
annotation.definitionFit: A slang phrase: 'the sauce' is alcohol, and a reformed drinker who returns to it is sliding back into the old habit.

entries.clue: The French could quarantine sick in this city (5)

indicatorNotes.could quarantine: to quarantine is to shut something away inside

blocks.note: le is French for the
sick means ill

annotation.surface: French authorities consider isolating the ill in one of their cities.
annotation.walkthrough: The French article supplies the outside letters, and the French setting of the surface also fits the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: Lille is a large city in northern France.

entries.clue: One getting high from, and later coming down on, H? (7)

annotation.definition: One getting high from, and later coming down on, H?

blocks.clueFragment: One getting high from, and later coming down on
blocks.note: the surface reads a drug user's high and comedown; really something rising into the air and landing
not heroin but the big H painted on a helipad

annotation.surface: A drug user gets high on heroin and then suffers the comedown.
annotation.walkthrough: H looks like heroin slang, but it is the H painted on a helipad, where a helicopter takes off and lands.
annotation.definitionFit: A chopper is a helicopter, which rises from and descends onto a helipad marked H.

entries.clue: Barking spaniel my boss subjected to discipline (9)

indicatorNotes.Barking: barking is British slang for mad, so the letters go mad

blocks.note: the letters of SPANIEL rearranged
the setter's boss is the editor, ED

annotation.surface: A noisy spaniel belonging to the speaker's boss gets told off.
annotation.walkthrough: Barking fits a dog, but here it means crazy. 'My boss' is the editor of the setter's newspaper.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the past participle: a player or employee given a punishment has been disciplined.

entries.clue: Implement gyration of booty (4)

indicatorNotes.gyration of: a gyration spins the word round

blocks.note: booty is loot

annotation.surface: An instruction to twerk.
annotation.walkthrough: Booty and gyration suggest a dance move, but booty is plunder here.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a hammer or a spade is both a tool and an implement, a hand-held thing for doing work.

entries.clue: Burning to get a hold of large queen for sure! (3,5)

indicatorNotes.to get a hold of: ALIGHT holds the letters inside it

blocks.note: burning means alight
L is the standard abbreviation for large
R is Regina, queen

annotation.surface: Someone is desperate to lay hands on a big queen, perhaps a drag star.
annotation.walkthrough: L and R go inside ALIGHT, after its first two letters.
annotation.definitionFit: 'All right!' is an exclamation of agreement, like 'for sure!'.

entries.clue: Incorrigible husband perhaps did some weeding topless (8)

indicatorNotes.topless: in a down entry the top is the first letter, which is removed

blocks.note: H is the standard abbreviation for husband
weeding is one kind of gardening, so GARDENED, minus its first letter

annotation.surface: A husband beyond reform does the weeding with his shirt off.
annotation.walkthrough: Topless paints a bare-chested gardener, but only takes the G off GARDENED; 'perhaps' marks weeding as one example of gardening.
annotation.definitionFit: A hardened criminal is set in his ways, incorrigible.

entries.clue: After turning over, make love with boss (4)

blocks.note: bonk is British slang for having sex

annotation.surface: Someone rolls over after sex with their employer.
annotation.walkthrough: Boss looks like the employer, but it is the other sense: a round stud or knob.
annotation.definitionFit: A boss is a round raised knob, as on a shield or ceiling.

entries.clue: Rats on board tucked into cream for the most part (7)

indicatorNotes.tucked into: TRAY is put inside the other letters
indicatorNotes.for the most part: most of BEST, so its last letter goes

blocks.note: a tray is a flat board for carrying things
the cream is the best; BEST without its last letter

annotation.surface: Rodents on a ship nibble at the dairy stores.
annotation.walkthrough: Rats reads as the animals but is the verb: to rat on someone is to betray them.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone who rats on friends betrays them.

entries.clue: One shielding joint quietly had knocked back a couple of lines (7)

blocks.note: p (piano) means quietly
had a meal means ate
A plus L and L, two lines

annotation.surface: A pot smoker quietly takes a drag on a joint, then snorts two lines of cocaine.
annotation.walkthrough: Joint, knocked back and lines all suggest drugs and drink; joint is the knee, and only 'a couple of lines' is reversed.
annotation.definitionFit: The patella, or kneecap, protects the front of the knee joint.

entries.clue: That Bow lass after wine becomes a fool (7)

indicatorNotes.after: the Bow lass comes after the wine, so ER is placed second

blocks.note: plonk is British slang for cheap wine
a Cockney from Bow would say 'er for her

annotation.surface: A girl from Bow makes an idiot of herself after drinking.
annotation.walkthrough: Bow is in the East End of London, and Cockneys drop the H, so 'that lass' there is 'ER. Plonker is British slang for an idiot.
annotation.definitionFit: British slang: plonker is a mild insult for a fool, made famous by the sitcom Only Fools and Horses.

entries.clue: One quickly kissing noble hugging man in pants? (6)

indicatorNotes.hugging: PEER hugs CK, wrapping round it

blocks.note: a peer is a nobleman
Calvin Klein, whose initials are on the waistband of underpants

annotation.surface: A lord in his underwear plants a hurried kiss on someone.
annotation.walkthrough: Pants are underpants in British English, and the man whose name is on them is Calvin Klein. Pecker also has a ruder sense that the surface nods at.
annotation.definitionFit: A quick kiss is a peck, so one who gives it is a pecker.

entries.clue: Go up and start on cast during a broadcast (6)

indicatorNotes.start on: the start of a word is its first letter
indicatorNotes.during: C comes during SEND, inside it

blocks.note: as printed
the first letter of cast
to broadcast is to send out

annotation.surface: Someone heads upstairs to get the actors going during a live show.
annotation.walkthrough: C goes inside SEND, and the leading A stays in front.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: climbing a staircase or a mountain is both going up and ascending it.

entries.clue: One supporting a painter's current work? (5)

annotation.definition: One supporting a painter's current work?

blocks.note: the surface suggests a patron backing an artist; really something physically holding a thing up
not the latest project but the actual canvas being painted right now

annotation.surface: A patron backing an artist's latest project.
annotation.walkthrough: Supporting reads as sponsoring, but it is physical: the easel holds the canvas being worked on.
annotation.definitionFit: An easel is the stand that holds a painter's canvas while it is being painted.

entries.clue: Tense trader's rear banker ruddy pinched on the sly (9)

indicatorNotes.rear: the rear of a word is its last letter

blocks.note: T is the standard abbreviation for tense
the last letter of trader
a banker is something with banks, a river; the Ouse is an English river
ruddy means red

annotation.surface: A nervous dealer's backside is secretly groped by a red-faced banker.
annotation.walkthrough: Banker is a crossword name for a river, the thing with banks. To trouser money is British slang for pocketing it, often dishonestly.
annotation.definitionFit: To trouser cash is to pocket it, so trousered means pinched on the sly.

entries.clue: Tender northern dons make some noise in bed? (5)

indicatorNotes.dons: SORE dons N, putting it on like a garment

blocks.note: tender means sore
N is the standard abbreviation for northern

annotation.surface: Amorous university lecturers from the north make a racket between the sheets.
annotation.walkthrough: Dons looks like academics, but it is the verb: to put on. The question mark hints the noise is not the one the surface suggests.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: snoring is one kind of noise a sleeper makes, and the question mark admits there are others.

entries.clue: Quickly look over small defender in reserves (5,4)

indicatorNotes.over: over means turned over, so PEEK becomes KEEP

blocks.note: a quick look is a peek; PEEK reversed
S is the standard abbreviation for small
a back is a defensive player in football

annotation.surface: A scout glances at a little defender in the reserve team.
annotation.walkthrough: Reserves reads as the second team, but it is the verb: to hold something back.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone who reserves something keeps it back.

entries.clue: Men brought back horse for a music producer (5)

indicatorNotes.brought back: brought back means turned round, so NAG becomes GAN

blocks.note: OR is other ranks, ordinary soldiers
a nag is a horse; NAG reversed

annotation.surface: Soldiers return a horse on behalf of a record producer.
annotation.walkthrough: A music producer looks like a studio job, but it is an instrument that produces music.
annotation.definitionFit: An organ is an instrument, something that produces music.

entries.clue: Fisherman in Ohio breaking flipping bones (3)

indicatorNotes.breaking: O breaks into RD, going inside it
indicatorNotes.flipping: flipping turns DR round to RD

blocks.note: bones, short for sawbones, is a doctor, DR; reversed
O is an abbreviation for Ohio

annotation.surface: An American angler breaks his damned bones.
annotation.walkthrough: Flipping is a mild British expletive in the surface; here it reverses DR. Rod can stand for the angler who wields one.
annotation.definitionFit: A rod is an angler, as in a stretch of river fished by six rods.

entries.clue: Denser idiot must get bewildered and confused (11)

indicatorNotes.bewildered: bewildered letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: the letters of DENSER IDIOT rearranged

annotation.surface: A particularly dim fool is bound to end up lost and muddled.
annotation.walkthrough: Bewildered and confused sit side by side as near-synonyms, but only the second is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: someone who has lost their bearings is muddled, so confused and disoriented are interchangeable.
